title: MV Why is SceneManager.renderScene() called on every requested frame?

posts.author: Mac15001900
posts.body:
TLDR: I've halved my game's CPU usage with one very simple change and I'm rather confused as to why this isn't the default.
So, this is something I've just noticed, and it rather stumped me.
SceneManager.updateMain
is a function that's called every frame, using
requestAnimationFrame
, and is primarily responsible for figuring out how many in-engine frames need to be processed. E.g. if 3/60th of a second passed since the last frame was ran, it will process 3 frames at once, but if less that 1/60th of a second has passed, it will process none.
Now, this makes perfect sense to me, but then at the end it goes on to call
this.renderScene()
... every time. Even if no frame has actually been processed, so it's just re-rendering everything even if nothing has changed. This means that, for example, on my 165Hz monitor the scene gets re-rendered 165 times per second, even though it only changes 60 times.
I've changed it so that it only calls
renderScene
if a new frame has actually been produced, and it more than halved my CPU usage (from 16% to 7% in the game's laggiest room) with no apparent ill effects. The game runs the same, the cursor still updates at 165fps since it's handled elsewhere.
Is there something I'm missing here? Is there some reason why it does that which I'm not aware of? Or is it just another case of core script writers not knowing that monitors with refresh rates above 60Hz exist?

Arthran said:
Graphics stuff isn't really my forte, but if I were to venture a guess as to why they would choose to do this, I'd say that it could be because they wanted to reduce the chances of screen tearing. Although screen tearing most commonly happens when the game renders faster than your monitor's refresh rate, it can also still happen (albeit less noticeably) when the reverse is true, because the graphics card might try to push a new frame to the monitor during the middle of a refresh cycle.
Click to expand...
Hmm.. I would have to disagree here.. if the scene is already rendered... re-rendering it when nothing has changed doesn't really change anything. it's like... having a sprite sheet where the first frame, and second frame are identical... nothing has changed from frame A -> frame B. Also this wouldn't necessarily mitigate screen tearing.. cause as before frame A -> frame B are the same.
Screen tearing occurs when the monitor begins drawing the contents of the game, BUT it's already finished drawing frame A but in the middle of drawing frame B... but again, if frame A and B are identical there's really nothing to tear to begin with...
Also the only way ensure screen tearing doesn't occur, is to ensure that the GPU is finished drawing the next frame, before the screen displays it, which this doesn't really do.. because it's simply rendering at the same rate as usual.. E.G. roughly every 16.6666666667 ms, so it's not really attempting to sync the gpu to the monitor in any way here. it's just rendering at the usual intervals, and if the GPU is rendering at the same set intervals, which are out of sync with the screens refresh rate, which is also at the same set intervals( whatever frame rate your monitor can display at ), then nothing is changing, and no attempt is made to "sync" the display
Anyone correct me if I'm wrong here on this ^^; I've not delved TOO heavily into vsync/gsync/freesync, but I have done.. a bit of research into it.
Also this is most definitely not an interpretation of vsync, vsync CAN be applied to an rpg maker game.. Actually again, correct me if I'm wrong again here, I believe vsync is enabled by default here via nwjs/chromium. It can be disabled via a special chromium flag "--disable-gpu-vsync"
Arthran said:
You are correct that MZ use's Pixi's ticker, whereas MV implements its own ticker using requestAnimationFrame. However, Pixi's ticker is also driven by requestAnimationFrame, and (to my understanding) both implementations should generally match the display's refresh rate.

Maybe I didn't explain myself well, or maybe I'm misunderstanding you, but I feel like you might be under the impression that I said the opposite of what I did (or what I intended to atleast).
I was not saying that re-rendering an identical frame could cause screen tearing--I was saying the opposite of that. I was saying that rendering a *changed* frame while the monitor is still in the process of drawing the previous frame could cause screen tearing.
My suggestion was that maybe the engine devs' thinking, when they chose to force a render every tick (instead of only after the game state has potentially changed), was that it could help prevent the chances of the rendering becoming misaligned with the monitor's refresh cycle, since it would then be rendering at the same rate that your monitor refreshes.
But all that being said, after having thought about it a bit more, I don't believe that it would really make a difference in this case. To my understanding, requestAnimationFrame is designed to synchronize with the monitor's refresh, so even when using Mac's modification, I think that the chances of misalignment occurring are probably pretty slim.

Screen tearing is the opposite of a screen lag - you're rendering the frames faster than your monitor can do it.
That being said, there's no way this is even remotely possible in MV's game loop.
MV is single-threaded and frame-capped at monitor's refresh rate. As such, there is never a situation where you'd be rendering two frames simultaneously. Because regardless when you push the new frame, the previous one will already have finished rendering.
